<reason>CON ran a sharp, well-written case built on the "toothless or cruel" dilemma against the passport lever, and drew a real concession from PRO that the off-list child comes home. But PRO answered squarely with A1/A2: deterrence via friction (slow adversarial parentage, liability, debarment) rather than statelessness, home-domiciled verification instruments (escrow, panel counsel, insurer files, revocation), and the flip that CON's own ban penalises the same adults at the same moment. CON's strongest counter (cheaper off-list clinic wins once deliverability is assured) was live, but CON then conceded "there is no mechanism" for the woman already pregnant and rested on unquantified volume reduction, which PRO undercut with the relocation history CON itself had cited (Thailand→Cambodia→Laos). PRO's closing weighing—leaky mechanism vs. no mechanism, and asymmetric downside if either side is wrong—made the decision easier. CON's clipped final turn and unanswered [B2.8] (altruistic surrogacy concession implies payment, not gestation, is the wrong) were minor additional costs. Clear but competitive win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A1 in Rebuttal 2 ([B4.1]-[B4.3]): rejecting CON's dilemma by reframing the sanction as friction plus liability rather than statelessness, then turning it—if judges blink at PRO's friction they blink at CON's fines, but PRO's surrogate still had escrow and counsel. CON's reply that blinking is child-harm-specific was fair, but the "child comes home" concession CON exploited was outweighed by CON's own "no mechanism" admission that PRO seized in closing.</best_rebuttal>
